#9734. The hidden features every Apple Maps user should know about

Apple Maps can warn you about traffic before you leave and remember where you parked.

Apple Maps didn't have a particularly auspicious start, with a notoriously rocky launch in 2012 that put it at an initial disadvantage against Google Maps. But Apple has rebuilt its map data since then and added many useful features such as detailed 3D buildings, cycling routes, curated guides and even a web version. With iOS 27, Apple Maps gained even more features, including AI-enhanced Flyover and Local Lists.

But there's more to Apple Maps than those headline features. Whether you're an Apple Maps fan looking to get even more out of the navigation app or need a few more reasons to give it another chance, there are a few lesser-known features you should know about. Now, whether it's better than Google Maps overall will depend on where you live and how you travel, and many drivers still prefer other navigation apps on CarPlay, but these at least show that Apple Maps has a lot to offer beyond basic navigation.

Frequent travelers often end up in areas without Wi-Fi or cell service, which makes navigation trickier. The good news is that Apple Maps lets you download entire regions for offline use, and it's super easy. Open Apple Maps on your iPhone and tap your profile picture next to the search bar, then select Offline Maps. Choose the area you want to download, and it'll save the map to your device, including infomation like place ratings, estimated arrival times and turn-by-turn directions. There's also an Only Use Offline Maps toggle for when you're on a limited data plan.

You can also easily write notes about places you've visited. Open any location in the Apple Maps app and tap the three-dot button. Tap Add a Note in the menu that appears. Apple says that your notes are kept private, so other Apple Maps users won't see them. You can find your notes every time you open that location on the map again.

Visited Places is also worth trying if you tend to forget the names of places you've been to. With this feature on, Apple Maps automatically remembers the places you've visited. In Maps, look for Visited Places under the Places section. You can store your visited places for three months, one year or forever. Unfortunately, this feature isn't available worldwide, but you can check whether you have it by going to Settings > Apps > Maps. Go to Location Services and turn on the Visited Places toggle.

The app also has a simple yet useful feature that helps you remember where you parked by dropping a pin when you disconnect from CarPlay and exit your car. To enable it, go to Settings > Apps > Maps and turn on Show Parked Location. If you don't use CarPlay, press and hold the Maps icon on the Home Screen and tap Mark Your Location to drop a pin at your current location.

Maps also has a feature that lets you help other drivers without taking your hands of the wheel. While driving, you can say, "Siri, there's an accident ahead" or "there's something on the road," and Siri will report the incident to other drivers. Incidents that Apple Maps supports include accidents, speed checks, heavy traffic and road closures. Like many of these features, though, availability will vary by location.

#9733. Crypto: Balancing Potential and Limitations – What Problems Can Digital Currencies Actually Solve?

The most enthusiastic crypto supporters once claimed (and some still do) that digital currencies can address all the flaws, risks, gaps, and shortcomings that burden the traditional financial system and that so many people are dissatisfied with. Except the reality has demonstrated they quite obviously can’t.

Crypto is indeed an exciting and promising innovation that has already proven it can be useful in many real-life situations, but that doesn’t automatically turn it into a fix-it-all. It’s not able to substitute fiat, nor can it single-handedly address issues like economic inequalities, structural inflation, security risks, and other similar problems.

However, if crypto were completely useless, we wouldn’t still be talking or hearing about it so often – but we are. If you want to know how far digital currencies have come and what’s happening in the crypto space at the moment, you can check out the Top Cryptocurrency News Today | Binance Square and read about the latest events and developments in the industry.

So, if crypto can’t bring world peace, what exactly can it do, and how far do its powers extend?

People were initially reluctant to engage with crypto and didn’t know what to make of it, but once the fear of the unknown subsided and curiosity took over, they realized that digital currencies possess certain qualities that can make them useful in various circumstances, as follows.

Diversification is a must in investment in order to reduce the risk of losses, and it relies on a simple principle of spreading capital across various types of assets with different risk profiles instead of concentrating it in a single one. Over the years, crypto has grown into quite a popular investment tool, even though it was intended to serve as a payment solution. Long story short, digital currencies have found their way into many investors’ holdings, and some of them have earned substantial profits from their crypto investments.

A portfolio can be well-balanced even if it doesn’t contain a single crypto, so digital assets aren’t a requirement for diversification. But the fact that they have a relatively low correlation to traditional markets, being driven by a different combination of factors, and can bring in outsized gains due to their sharp price swings makes them a good choice in this respect. Nevertheless, experts recommend keeping crypto allocations low (between 1% and 5% of a total portfolio) to protect against volatility risks.

Crypto is powered by blockchain technology, which means issuance and transactions are managed by a network of nodes instead of a single central entity, like governments, banks, and payment processors. This unique structure gives crypto the possibility to help with economic mobility.

By removing the intermediaries, coins can be transferred directly from one person to another, so the funds can arrive in the recipient’s wallet almost instantly, whereas with fiat, it can take up to several days for transactions to be processed, especially for international transfers that involve more cumbersome bureaucratic procedures.

Transaction speed is not the only aspect that crypto can improve, but affordability as well. Because there are no middlemen to incur processing fees, transferring crypto is cheaper than transferring conventional currencies.

And let’s not forget about all the people in the world who can’t use banking services because of all the barriers they impose. Crypto is easily accessible to everyone as long as they have a smart device and internet connection.

Another advantage that derives from crypto’s decentralized architecture is the ability to conceal users’ real identity. Crypto wallets are pseudonymous, so holders are not required to share sensitive data like legal names and personal addresses in order to use crypto. The blockchain also offers a public record of all the transactions it has ever processed, giving everyone the possibility to verify transfers and offering a level of transparency that fiat money cannot match.

The advantages that crypto offers seem absolutely amazing, but volatility casts a shadow over all these perks. Digital currencies can be a good addition to investors’ holdings, as they can offer high growth, but if the allocations are not well balanced, a market downturn can drag the entire portfolio down.

At the same time, the alleged decentralization that removes intermediaries from the equation and makes crypto transactions faster and cheaper in theory doesn’t always apply in practice. In many situations, crypto transactions run through centralized exchanges, or the projects are controlled by a foundation or corporate entity, which goes against the decentralization ethos that digital assets promote. So, instead of offering a different path to transferring value than traditional finance, crypto often uses the same centralized mechanism.

Using crypto to pay for goods and services is not practical because, once again, volatility gets in the way. With crypto values shifting constantly, it’s extremely challenging for companies that accept crypto payments to price their products and protect their profits. Many resort to payment processors to help them deal with volatility, but that kind of contradicts the whole idea of embracing crypto to bypass the middlemen.

It’s bold, if not downright absurd, to say that crypto can provide the answer to all of society’s money-related problems. But it’s equally absurd to dismiss it as a useless tool when it’s already being used in so many areas, and its integration into global finance continues to grow. Digital currencies can step in instances and areas where conventional banking services are either absent or highly inefficient. The takeaway here is that they can only serve as a complementary solution, not a complete replacement for traditional financial systems.

#9732. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9730. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

#9728. Your H-1B starts October 1. You may enter up to 10 days early, but you cannot work yet

Checked against official sources on November 15, 2026

Your H-1B approval notice has a start date. Say it is October 1. You want to fly in a week early, find a place, and get set up. Can you enter? And can you start work that same week?

The rule answers both questions. You may be allowed to enter early. You may not start work before the petition's start date.

An H-1B worker, and that worker's H-4 family, may be admitted to the United States for the dates on the petition. They may also be admitted up to 10 days before those dates begin, and up to 10 days after they end. The same extra days may also be given when U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) grants the status inside the country.

You may not work in those extra days. Work is allowed only during the validity period of the petition, unless a separate work rule applies.

This is not the 60-day period that can follow a job ending. That is a different rule, in the next paragraph of the same section. This post is about the 10-day periods only.

The rule is in the U.S. immigration regulations, at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(1). The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) set this text in a final rule published in the Federal Register on November 18, 2016. The rule took effect on January 17, 2017. The current eCFR still carries that text.

Here is the work sentence, as the regulation writes it: "Unless authorized under 8 CFR 274a.12, the alien may not work except during the validity period."

In that same final rule, DHS described these extra days. The days before the start give a reasonable amount of time to enter the United States and prepare to begin employment. The days after the end give a reasonable amount of time to depart. They also give a reasonable amount of time to take other actions to extend, change, or otherwise maintain lawful status.

The rule uses "up to" 10 days, and it uses "may." It does not promise that every person will receive a full 10 days.

A later sentence sits at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(3). It says a person in any authorized period in paragraph (l) may apply for an extension of stay or a change of status. That person must still be otherwise eligible.

Say the petition is valid from October 1. The rule allows admission up to 10 days before that date. If the full 10 days are given, that window opens on September 21.

Those days are for arriving and getting settled. DHS said they help a person be ready to start work when the petition begins. They are not work days. Starting the job on September 25 would be work outside the validity period.

The officer at the border or airport decides your admission. The rule says "may" and "up to." After you enter, check the I-94 you received. The authorized stay is the date on that record.

The same rule allows up to 10 days after the petition's end date. DHS said this time is to leave the United States, or to take other steps to extend, change, or keep lawful status. You still may not work in those days, unless a separate work authorization applies.

If your job has ended, or if an extension is still waiting for a decision, other rules may also apply. Those rules are not the subject of this post. For a question about your own end date, speak with a licensed immigration attorney.

This post shares general information from official U.S. government pages. TalentOp Systems LLC is not giving legal advice here. Rules can change, and every case is different. For a question about your own situation, please speak with a licensed immigration attorney.

#9726. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

#9725. Why a canvas re-encode can make a JPEG bigger

Disclosure: This report on the image-processing tests run by the LighterPics project was written with AI assistance.

Exporting an existing JPEG through a canvas does not guarantee a smaller file. At quality 0.92, five of 25 test photos grew in Chromium, 10 in Firefox and 11 in WebKit.

All three ran the same photos at the same requested quality. For every photo, the Firefox and WebKit JPEGs were larger than the Chromium JPEG. The quality argument alone was not enough to predict the output size across engines.

A canvas export starts from decoded pixels and creates a new file. Its size depends on the output format, encoder settings and image content. The API does not promise to keep it below the input byte count.

The converter used createImageBitmap() followed by a canvas export. Its quality settings were passed to toBlob() or the equivalent worker export; PNG does not use that argument. [1]

Chromium ran the wider quality sweep. Here are the results for the 25 JPEG photos:

At JPEG 0.70, no photo grew and the median output size was 26% of the input. No photo grew at any of the lower tested JPEG quality values either.

At JPEG quality 1.0, the median output was nearly twice the input size. That setting requests the highest quality, but it still re-encodes the decoded image and cannot recover detail lost in the original JPEG. The recorded median PSNR, a measure of pixel error against the decoded input, was 56.88 dB at 1.0, 43.33 dB at 0.92 and 40.29 dB at 0.80. These were objective measurements, not a visual preference test.

WebP at 1.0 took a different path in this Chromium build: all 25 files contained the lossless VP8L bitstream. At 0.92, they contained lossy VP8. The WebP container specification distinguishes these two formats. [2]

Firefox also produced three larger files out of 25 at WebP 0.92, with a median size of 50% of the input. WebKit produced no accepted WebP output. PNG made every photo larger in all three engines; the Firefox and WebKit medians were 383% and 421%, respectively.

The five photos that grew at JPEG 0.92 in Chromium also grew in Firefox and WebKit. Four were night shots and one was a portrait. They were among the inputs with the fewest bytes per pixel, but that alone did not explain the result: the lowest-bytes-per-pixel photo shrank in Chromium. The tests did not record encoder libraries or chroma subsampling, so they do not identify the cause of the engine differences.

The compressor searched for an output that fit a requested byte budget. Across 1,407 Chromium runs that produced a file, it returned 177 files larger than their inputs. Every one had a target at or above the input size.

A re-encoded file can fit the requested budget while still exceeding the original size.

In JPEG mode, the compressor first tries quality 0.92. If that output fits, it returns it; otherwise it searches lower qualities and, when allowed, reduces the pixel dimensions. The WebP and MozJPEG traces also started at 0.92 for the runs that produced larger files.

Of the 177 larger outputs, 159 came from the first encode at 0.92. The other 18 came from searches that settled between 0.75 and 0.91. All met the target, but none reduced the input byte count.

Reducing pixel dimensions helped when the target was below the input size: the compressor met the target in 543 of 549 runs with resizing allowed, compared with 230 of 489 without it. Successful runs in that group reached a median of 98.4% of the target. When the target was missed, the tool returned its smallest attempt; those outputs still did not exceed the input size in this test set.

For the single cross-engine compressor setting, JPEG with a 200 KB target and resizing allowed, all 25 photos came in under the target in every engine. That result does not extend to all targets or settings.

If a tool must never increase file size, it needs a separate comparison against the input byte count. Checking only the requested target is insufficient.

Converting PNG to JPEG was not a reliable way to shrink the generated screenshots and graphics. At JPEG 0.92 in Chromium, four of five screenshots grew, with a median output size of 122% of the input. Three of five graphics grew, with a median of 110%.

A separate test first converted each of the 25 photos to WebP at 0.80. Those WebPs were a median of 23% of the original JPEG size. Converting them again made every file larger than its intermediate WebP:

These ratios use the intermediate WebP as the reference file.

This short example uses one of the photos that grew at JPEG 0.92. Open about:blank in a desktop browser and paste it into the DevTools console. The Wikimedia file server allows the cross-origin request.

The input is 878,879 bytes. The recorded outputs were:

At JPEG 0.92, Firefox produced 1,557,092 bytes and WebKit 1,690,770 bytes.

In the recorded snippet check on 2026-11-11, every output size with a harness counterpart matched: all four settings in Chromium, and JPEG 0.92 and PNG in Firefox and WebKit. Different browser builds may produce different sizes.

The harness built LighterPics locally and called the processing functions and Web Workers used by its tool pages. The runs used Playwright 1.58.2 on an Apple M3 Pro, macOS Darwin 25.6.0, arm64. The engines were the headless Playwright builds named above, not the corresponding branded releases. [3]

Inputs were 25 CC0 JPEG photos from Wikimedia Commons, checked against their SHA-256 hashes, plus five generated PNG screenshots and five generated PNG graphics for the Chromium tests. The photos ranged from 316,480 to 5,603,777 bytes and from 3.15 to 12.19 megapixels.

Chromium ran 10 JPEG and 10 WebP quality settings plus PNG. Firefox and WebKit ran JPEG 0.92, WebP 0.92 and PNG. The compressor sweep was Chromium-only: seven targets from 20 to 2,000 KB, with resizing enabled and disabled, using canvas JPEG, canvas WebP and WebAssembly MozJPEG. Here, 1 KB means 1,000 bytes. An additional 63 MozJPEG runs failed on the pixel limit with resizing disabled and are excluded from the 1,407 runs with output.

The project page publishes selected Chromium summaries. The cross-engine results and some other figures in this article are held only in the private result files listed below. [4]

These are observations from one machine and a small input set. Other browser versions, operating systems and photos may produce different results. There was no human assessment of visual quality, and matching a size target should not be read as preserving acceptable image quality.

Run records The main Chromium run used site and harness commit eacd79c, harness version 1.1.0, on 2026-11-10. The WebP-then-convert run used harness 1e3cf33 with the same site code. The cross-engine run used harness 349005d, version 1.2.0, on 2026-11-11. The results are stored in results-2026-11-10-r5.json, results-2026-11-10-webp.json and results-2026-11-11-metadata.json. The WebP-then-convert run and cross-engine run have repeat files; the main Chromium run was not repeated at this code version. The repository and raw results are private.

The main Chromium run used site and harness commit eacd79c, harness version 1.1.0, on 2026-11-10. The WebP-then-convert run used harness 1e3cf33 with the same site code. The cross-engine run used harness 349005d, version 1.2.0, on 2026-11-11.

The results are stored in results-2026-11-10-r5.json, results-2026-11-10-webp.json and results-2026-11-11-metadata.json. The WebP-then-convert run and cross-engine run have repeat files; the main Chromium run was not repeated at this code version. The repository and raw results are private.

The WebP 1.0 result is the most instructive detail, because a lossless VP8L bitstream at maximum quality explains why all 25 files grew to a 250% median instead of shrinking. The finding that the same five night photos grew at JPEG 0.92 across all three engines also suggests the input content matters as much as the encoder, since noisy or high-frequency detail survives poorly through a second quantisation pass. For a browser tool, the practical rule seems clear: never return a re-encoded file without comparing it with the original byte count, and treat a size target as a budget rather than a guarantee. Would a lower starting point such as JPEG 0.80, which had a 39% median and only two growing files, be a safer default for photos, reserving 0.92 for cases where visible quality differences are actually measured?

#9724. My journey so far as a fresh man software wngeneering student

My name is Bona Hanson Junior and i study sofware engeneering at YIBS-ISSEST.Starting university as a Software Engineering student has been an exciting and challenging experience for me.

When I first entered this field, I knew I was stepping into a world full of technology, innovation, and endless possibilities. However, I quickly realized that Software Engineering is much more than just writing lines of code. It requires patience, creativity, logical thinking, and a willingness to learn.

My journey started with learning the fundamentals of programming, algorithms, computer systems, and problem-solving.

At first, some concepts seemed complicated(especially maths). Understanding how algorithms work, writing my first programs, and figuring out how different parts of a computer interact were all new experiences.

But every lecture and practical exercise introduced me to something new.

One of the most interesting parts of my journey so far has been learning C programming.

Using tools like Visual Studio Code and exploring Git and GitHub have helped me understand how developers write, manage, and share code.

Of course, it hasn't always been easy. There have been moments when my code refused to work, when I couldn't understand an error, or when I spent more time debugging than actually writing code.

Every error is an opportunity to learn something new.

Being a freshman means having a lot to discover. Sometimes things get difficult, but I'm gradually learning that:

I know I still have a long way to go. I'm not an expert, and I don't pretend to know everything.

I'm simply a Software Engineering student eager to learn, improve my skills, build meaningful projects, and explore the endless possibilities of technology.

My goal is to turn the knowledge I gain today into practical skills that will help me create solutions tomorrow.

I'm excited to share my progress, document my learning experiences, connect with other developers, and grow within the tech community.

I'm always happy to connect with fellow students, developers, mentors, and technology enthusiasts. Let's learn, share knowledge, and grow together.All helps and new tips on how to improve my software engeneering knowledge would be nice

#9721. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9719. GitHub Actions Unable to resolve action, and which half failed

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at latchkey.dev

GitHub Actions Unable to resolve action appears in two forms, and the difference between them is the whole diagnosis: one says the repository could not be found, and the other says the repository was found but the ref you asked for was not. Nothing downloads and no action code runs in either case, because the reference is resolved before anything is fetched.

Two endings, two stopping points. Repository not found means the path never resolved; unable to find version means it did and the ref did not.

A step fails at the very start with a single line and no other output. There is no setup log for the action, no inputs echoed, nothing from the action itself, because the action was never obtained. The step that fails is often one nobody touched, in a workflow that has been green for months, which makes a repository rename or a deleted tag the first thing to suspect rather than the workflow file.

``Quoted from gigalixir/gigalixir-action#67, reported verbatim by the user Error: Unable to resolve actiongigalixir/gigalixir-action@v1, unable to find versionv1`

A commit SHA cannot be moved or deleted by the action's maintainer, which removes this whole failure mode for that step. The documentation recommends it as the safest reference for stability and security, and a dependency updater can still raise pull requests to advance it.

```.github/workflows/ci.yml (illustrative)

Checking the action out and calling it with a relative path avoids the action lookup entirely, because the reference resolves against the workspace. This is the right shape for an action that has no reason to be discoverable outside the repository.

```.github/workflows/ci.yml (illustrative)

Both forms open the same way, so the informative part is what comes after the reference. An ending of "repository not found" means the owner and repository part of your uses value did not resolve to something the run is allowed to see. An ending of "unable to find version" means it did resolve, and the tag, branch or commit after the @ did not exist there.

That split maps to two different searches. For the first, whose reported form is Error: Unable to resolve action. Repository not found: ytanikin/PRConventionalCommits, check the spelling and case of the path, check whether the repository was renamed or made private, and check whether this run has access to it at all. For the second, the repository is fine and you are looking at a tag question: a major version tag that was never published, a tag that was deleted or moved, or a branch that was renamed.

Resolution happens before any download, which is why neither form leaves a partial log. The runner collects the references a job needs and asks the service to resolve them, and a failure there means the job stops with one line rather than with a half-downloaded action.

Renames are the version of this that looks least like a mistake. GitHub redirects browser and clone traffic for a renamed repository, and a uses reference to the old name can still fail to resolve, which is why a workflow that has not changed starts failing on a step nobody edited.

The convention that uses: owner/action@v3 keeps working is a convention, not a guarantee. It relies on the action's maintainer publishing and moving a lightweight v3 tag alongside each v3.x.y release, and the documentation says as much: it notes that the behavior of major version tags is at the discretion of the action's author.

So a README instructing you to use @v3 can be ahead of the tags, behind them, or simply wrong, and the failure you get names the version rather than the README. Two public reports quoted in this hub are exactly that: a README saying @v1 for an action whose v1 tag had not been published, and another saying @v3 for the same reason.

The response is not to avoid major tags, which are genuinely useful, but to verify the ref exists when you first add it and to know that a pin to a commit SHA is the only reference that cannot be moved out from under you. The documentation recommends the SHA for stability and security for that reason.

`Terminal gh api repos/OWNER/ACTION/git/matching-refs/tags/v --jq '.[].ref' `

When the action lives in a private repository in your own organization, the failing form is usually repository not found, which reads as though the path is wrong. The path is fine. What is missing is that the repository holding the action has not allowed its workflows and actions to be used by other repositories in the organization, which is a setting on the action's repository rather than on the workflow's.

This one is worth stating plainly because the instinct is to reach for a token. A personal access token with repository access does not change the answer, because the resolution is not a clone you are authenticating: it is the service deciding whether this run may use that action. The fix is a setting.

The alternative, which avoids the question entirely, is to check the action out into the workspace and call it by a relative path. A local uses: ./path reference resolves against the checked out repository rather than through the action lookup, and it is the pattern to reach for when an action is genuinely internal.

Both forms of the message are produced when the run resolves its action references, which happens before the action is downloaded and therefore before there is anything for a runner to log beyond the one line. A Latchkey recording would consist of that line and nothing else.

More to the point, producing one means writing a workflow that references a repository or a tag that does not exist, which is manufacturing the evidence rather than observing it. Both forms are quoted here from public reports where real repositories and real missing tags produced them, which is a stronger provenance than a failure we would have staged.

Most often because something changed on the other end: a major version tag was deleted or moved during a release, a branch was renamed, or the repository itself was renamed or made private. The reference in your file is static, and everything it points at belongs to somebody else.

No. Resolving an action reference is not a clone you authenticate, it is the service deciding whether this run may use that action. The setting lives on the repository that holds the action, allowing its actions and workflows to be used by other repositories in the organization.

For anything you depend on, yes. A SHA cannot be moved or deleted by the maintainer, which removes this failure entirely for that step, and the documentation recommends it as the safest reference. Keep a comment naming the version so the pin stays readable, and let a dependency updater advance it.

#9717. My Local AI Agent Needed a Bigger Brain, So I Gave It a Decentralized GPU

Nosana is an open-source GPU cloud for AI and high-performance workloads, offering lower-cost instant compute.

this is my second progress update for the Decentralize AI Hackathon by HackerNoon and Nosana.

In my first article, I Built a Local AI Linux Assistant That Doesn't Rely on the Cloud, I introduced zkzkAgent: an AI agent that manages a Linux machine through plain language and runs entirely on my own hardware with Ollama.

That is still how it works by default. But running everything locally has a ceiling, and I kept hitting it.

To test the integration in real work, I switched to the 27B model on Nosana and gave zkzkAgent a task: create a new project called zkzk_ai, a calculator web app with a FastAPI backend and an HTML, CSS, and JavaScript frontend, and open it in VS Code.

The classifier sent the request to the planner (`NEEDS_PLANNING`). The planner wrote a 9-step plan, including the full content of every file, and then stopped and waited for me:

Once I approved the plan, the executor got to work. It made 10 tool calls, one at a time, across 10 graph iterations (with a maximum of 15).

Wrote static/index.html (2,396 characters)

Wrote static/style.css (1,563 characters)

Wrote static/script.js (2,655 characters)

Nothing complicated happens behind the scenes. The model running on Nosana picks a tool; that tool executes on my machine, and the result is sent back to the model.

To make this clearer, here's an actual example from the execution log (trimmed for readability):Each call follows the same loop. The model on Nosana picks the next tool, the tool runs on my machine, and the result goes back into the conversation. In the log, one turn of that loop looks like this (trimmed):

Next, I asked: "Can you change the zkzk_ai Calculator to be zkzk?" The classifier sent this to the planner as well, which wrote a 7-step plan. After I approved it, the agent read static/index.html and then changed the name in three places: the page title and heading, the FastAPI app title, and the README. It did not touch the calculator logic.

I started the app with `uvicorn app:app`. The page loaded, and the calculator API answered:

Across both requests, every model call in the saved log, 18 in total, went to `inference.nosana.com` and returned `200 OK`. Every file write, command, and app launch happened locally.

I reviewed the code the agent wrote, and tested the backend directly:

- No eval. Expressions are parsed with Python's ast module, and only numbers, parentheses, and `+ - * / // % **` are allowed. When I sent __import__("os"), it was rejected with "Unsupported expression element: Call".

- Clear errors. Division by zero and complex results (such as (-1)**0.5) return a readable message instead of crashing.

- Input limits. Expressions are capped at 500 characters in both the browser and the API.

- Keyboard support. Enter evaluates, Backspace deletes, Esc clears and `^` types a power.

The code is on GitHub at [zkzkGamal/calculator], and the full run log is in the [zkzkAgent repo]

My first article was about an agent that doesn't rely on the cloud. This update doesn't change that. It adds a choice. Private or sensitive work stays on local Ollama, where nothing leaves the machine. Heavy planning can use a much larger model on Nosana's network instead of a centralized provider. In both modes, the tools, the files, and the final yes stay with me.

1. A real benchmark. Run the same five tasks on the local 2B model and on the 27B model on Nosana, and measure success rate, tool calls, time, tokens, and cost. Numbers instead of impressions.

2. Hybrid routing. Because the graph has separate nodes, each node can use its own model. The classifier and chat replies are short and could stay on a small local model, while the planner and executor use Nosana. Plain conversations would then never leave the machine.

3. Automatic fallback. If Nosana can't be reached, switch to local Ollama automatically, the same way the agent already turns Wi-Fi back on by itself.

4. Close the safety gaps. Enforce plan-level confirmations. Also put `run_command` behind a confirmation or an allow-list: today it can run any shell command, and with a remote model choosing the arguments, that matters more than before.

5. Fix the calculator bug with the agent doing the fix.

#9716. How do you efficiently manage and restore distinct authentication states when running Playwright tests in parallel?

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at styrow.dev

🔥 Playwright Parallel Testing Headache: How do you efficiently manage and restore distinct authentication states when running Playwright tests in parallel? Sharing auth across parallel test workers causes flaky failures and slow execution.

💡 Solution & Code Walkthrough The robust solution leverages Playwright's browserContext with storageState. This strategy ensures each parallel test worker has its own isolated, pre-authenticated session.

Step 1: Create an auth.setup.ts script This runs once to log in a user and save their session state.

Step 2: Configure playwright.config.ts to use storageState This tells Playwright to load the saved state for all tests.

Step 3: Write your tests (they now run pre-authenticated!)

🔑 Key Takeaways ✅ Isolation: Each test runs in its own distinct, pre-authenticated browserContext. ✅ Efficiency: No need to re-login in every test or worker, significantly speeding up parallel runs. ✅ Robustness: Eliminates cross-test authentication pollution, reducing flakiness. • The setup project ensures authentication runs once before dependent tests.

TAGS: playwright, testing, automation, typescript, authentication, parallel testing, e2e, ci/cd

#9713. GitHub Actions env var with special characters in a run step

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at latchkey.dev

A GitHub Actions env var with special characters breaks a run step because of an ordering detail that is easy to have backwards: an expression is substituted into the script as text before any shell is started, so the shell parses your value as if you had typed it. Quoting the reference in the script does not help, because by then the value is the script.

Substitution happens while the script file is written. The shell is started afterwards and sees only the finished text.

A run step fails with a shell syntax error that quotes a fragment of somebody commit message, a branch name or a pull request title. The message often mentions an unexpected end of file while looking for a matching quote, which is the shell telling you it reached the end of the script still waiting for something to close. The workflow is unchanged from yesterday. What changed is the data, and that is the tell: a step that breaks on one branch and works on another is being fed, not misconfigured.

``Reconstructed from a bash syntax error; the temporary script name differs on every run /home/runner/work/_temp/f1c2.sh: line 2: unexpected EOF while looking for matching"'

When the destination is an action, put the expression under with. No shell parses that path, so the whole class of problem disappears rather than being contained.

Set the environment variable to a literal containing a double quote, a single quote, a dollar sign, a backtick and a newline, and run the step. A fix that survives that string will survive a commit message.

A run step is not handed to a shell as a command line. The runner evaluates the expressions in the step, writes the resulting text into a temporary script file, and then starts the shell with that file as its argument. Everything an expression produced is part of the file by the time the shell opens it.

That ordering decides the whole problem. An expression that produces a value containing a double quote does not produce a string containing a quote, it produces a script with an extra quote in it. The shell then reads a script whose quoting is unbalanced and reports a syntax error against a line number in a temporary file, which is why the error names a path under the runner work directory that you cannot open.

It also explains why the usual instinct fails. Wrapping the expression in quotes inside the script only changes where the extra quote lands. If the value can contain the character you are quoting with, no amount of quoting in the script text is safe, because the value is not being quoted, it is being pasted.

The consequence beyond broken syntax is the more serious one. A value that can close a quote can also start a command, so this is the same mechanism behind script injection through workflow data, and the fix is the same fix.

The third row is the whole fix. The value reaches the process through the environment, which is a channel the shell does not parse, and the script contains only a variable name.

Map the expression to an environment variable on the step, then read that variable in the script with the reference quoted. The script text now contains a variable name and nothing else, so the content of the value cannot change how the script parses. The shell looks the variable up at run time and hands the contents to the command as one argument.

The quoting in the script still matters, but for a much smaller reason. An unquoted variable reference is subject to word splitting and filename expansion, so a value with spaces becomes several arguments and a value containing an asterisk may become a list of file names. Quoting the reference stops both. It cannot fix a value pasted in as text, which is why the two steps go together rather than either one alone.

For printing, prefer a command that takes a format string and treats its arguments as data. Echo behaves differently across shells with values that begin with a dash or contain backslashes, and a format based print avoids the whole category.

Anything a person can write. Commit messages, branch and tag names, pull request titles and bodies, issue titles, review comments and the display names attached to all of them. These arrive through the event payload and they are exactly the values people paste into scripts, because they are the interesting ones.

Values that come from your own configuration deserve the same handling for a duller reason: they change. A variable holding a version string is safe until somebody puts a space in it, and the step that has worked for a year fails on the day it does.

Multi line values deserve a note of their own. A commit message body contains newlines, and a newline pasted into a script is a new command. Passed through the environment it is just a character in the value, which is the behavior you wanted.

Where a value is going to a step that takes inputs rather than to a shell, pass it under with instead. No shell is involved at all in that path, so nothing parses it.

A recorded run would show a shell syntax error against a temporary script whose name is generated per run, and the interesting half of the evidence, the script the runner actually wrote, is not in the log. Showing the error without the generated script would be showing the least informative part of the failure.

The mechanism is better argued from the ordering itself, which is visible in how a run step is executed: expressions are evaluated into the script file, and the shell is started against that file afterwards. Once that order is clear, every symptom on this page follows from it without needing a demonstration.

There is no repair either, and it is worth being plain about why. A runner cannot re quote a script it did not write on your behalf, and guessing which fragment was data and which was code is precisely the ambiguity that caused the failure.

Because the expression is substituted before any shell exists. The runner writes the evaluated text into a script file and then starts a shell on that file, so your quotes and the value end up side by side in the same text. A quote inside the value closes yours.

Map it to an environment variable in the step env block and read that variable with the reference quoted. The value then travels through the environment, which the shell does not parse, and the script contains only the variable name.

Only if the value reached the script through the environment. Quoting stops word splitting and filename expansion of an expansion, which is worth doing, but it cannot protect a value that was pasted into the script text before the shell started.

Because the data changed rather than the workflow. The step breaks the first time somebody writes a quote, a backtick or a bracket in the branch name or commit message it reads, which is why the failure looks random and is not.

#9712. Why Your NumPy Array Changed After Preprocessing (Views vs Copies in ML)

Student focused on web development and programming. I write about debugging, coding challenges, and improving skills.

Student focused on web development and programming. I write about debugging, coding challenges, and improving skills.

Student focused on web development and programming. I write about debugging, coding challenges, and improving skills.

A small NumPy operation can modify data you never intended to touch. Understanding views, copies, and memory sharing can prevent silent bugs in machine learning pipelines.

Imagine preparing a dataset for a machine learning model. You load the original data, select a few columns, normalize their values, and pass the result to your training algorithm.

Later, when you inspect the original dataset, something looks wrong. Some values have changed, even though you never directly modified the original array.

This is one of those Python behaviors that can make debugging surprisingly difficult. The problem usually comes down to how NumPy handles memory. When you create a new array from an existing one, NumPy does not always allocate new memory. Sometimes, it creates a view that points to the same underlying data.

This matters most during preprocessing, where slicing, normalization, reshaping, and feature selection are common. Let’s look at why it happens, how to detect it, and how to avoid it.

A view creates a new array object that shares memory with another array.

A copy creates a separate array with its own data.

The original array changed even though we modified only the view variable. Basic slicing creates a view, so both arrays reference the same memory for the selected elements.

The original array is unchanged. The difference isn’t in the variable names or values. It’s in how NumPy manages memory. If you’ve seen the same idea with plain Python lists, see Why .copy() in Python Still Mutates Your Original List.

Machine learning preprocessing often involves selecting features and transforming numerical values.

Suppose the first two columns are features you want to center around zero. A developer might write:

But the original dataset has also changed:

Slicing created a view of data. Then features -= ... modified the values in place, and since features and data share memory, the change appeared in both.

This is especially dangerous when the original dataset is needed for another preprocessing step, a model comparison, or evaluation.

The processed features are transformed, and the original dataset stays intact.

This .copy() call makes the intent explicit: the preprocessing should work on independent data. Copying everything is not always necessary, though, because it increases memory usage, especially with large datasets. The better habit is knowing when NumPy shares memory and when it doesn’t.

NumPy provides np.shares_memory() for this:

You can also inspect the .base attribute:

The .base attribute shows which array owns the memory behind a view, but it isn’t a complete test for memory sharing. For reliable checks, use np.shares_memory().

A common mistake is assuming that any operation returning a new array creates independent memory. Different operations behave differently:

The key distinction is basic indexing versus advanced indexing.

Basic slicing returns a view, and advanced indexing returns a copy. Two expressions that look like they do the same selection can behave differently in memory, so don’t assume that selecting elements creates independent data.

The difference between in-place and regular arithmetic matters just as much:

In the second version, view + 5 produces a new result, and the name view is rebound to it. The original array is untouched.

Preprocessing code often uses in-place operations to save memory:

If features is a view, the original data changes too.

A typical pipeline includes selecting features, handling missing values, scaling numerical columns, encoding categories, splitting data, and preparing arrays for training. Shared memory can cause trouble at several of these steps.

Problem 1: Accidentally modifying the original dataset. If preprocessing changes the original array, later experiments may use altered values instead of the initial data. Results become hard to reproduce.

Problem 2: Modifying shared training data. If your train and test arrays are views of the same source, an in-place transformation on one can silently change the other. This is a memory-sharing bug, not data leakage, but it can produce results that look valid while being wrong.

Data leakage is a separate issue. It happens when information from the test set influences training, for example by fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting. The correct approach is to split first, fit preprocessing only on the training data, and then apply the learned transformation to the test data.

Many scikit-learn transformers, such as StandardScaler, return new arrays by default, so this bug is less common there. Some of them accept a copy=False argument, though, and hand-written in-place NumPy code doesn’t protect you at all.

Problem 3: Difficult debugging. The code runs without errors. The model trains, predictions look reasonable, and metrics seem plausible. The real problem may be hidden in a preprocessing step earlier in the pipeline.

If the original must stay unchanged, make an explicit copy:

Then transform the independent array. For large datasets, weigh the memory cost before copying everything.

NumPy views and copies look similar at first. Both are new variables, both can hold the same values, and both can be passed into machine learning functions. Their memory behavior is different.

A view shares memory with its source, while a copy owns its data. That difference becomes critical when preprocessing uses in-place operations.

The main lesson: don’t assume a new variable means new memory. When a dataset changes unexpectedly, check how the array was created before blaming the preprocessing formula, the model, or the data itself.

Sometimes, the fix is just one missing .copy().

#9711. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.
