#9710. Perplexica's Title Matches Need an Authentication Check Before They Become a Search Inventory

Perplexica is an open-source AI search interface. A ZoomEye count-only probe on November 15, 2026 returned no app="Perplexica" matches, 586 title="Perplexica" matches, and 662 http.body="Perplexica" matches. The queries used sub_type=all, page 1, and page size 1.

The title and body counts are close, which can invite a false sense of precision. Both are textual observations. A deployment page, a project fork, a documentation site, and a live search interface can all carry the name. The absent application fingerprint means the engine did not identify the app signature for this query; it does not mean no instance exists.

An AI search interface combines a web search source, a model provider, prompt construction, and a conversation state. The public page may only expose the question box, while the server holds API credentials for search and model services. Review those credentials as separate assets.

If the service is intended for a trusted team, put authentication in front of the search endpoint and the administration paths. A public demo can be acceptable when it has its own budget, rate limits, and a clear statement that questions are not private. A private deployment should not inherit the demo's access model.

Watch outbound network policy. A search tool can fetch URLs as part of answering a question. That behavior may create server-side request forgery risk if the destination is not controlled. Restrict which search backends and model endpoints the application can reach, and keep provider keys out of client-side code.

The product repository is the best place to confirm supported deployment and configuration. Do not infer a live deployment from a title alone. A matching title might be a fork's README on a code-hosting page. Confirm that the response contains an application interface and that the service has a real request path.

For a confirmed instance, record whether authentication is enabled, which search engine and model are configured, whether sessions are stored, and how long queries and answers are retained. A generic search service can expose user interests even when it does not store a user account.

Rate limiting should apply to questions, model calls, and outbound fetch attempts. A single expensive query can consume provider budget or tie up a worker. Add per-IP and per-user limits where identity exists, and a global concurrency cap where identity does not.

The 586 title and 662 body matches are close enough to compare, but they should not be added together. The same host may appear in both, and a documentation page may account for many body hits. Keep the exact dorks and timestamps with the finding.

Start with title matches that return a search page. Filter out repositories and documentation by checking the final URL and response type. If the service has a login prompt, record the authentication method and avoid testing credentials. Ask the owner whether the instance is a demo, a team tool, or a public service.

Monitor changes around known deployment domains. A new title match can indicate a migration. It can also be a status page that copied the product name. A missing match can reflect a response change rather than a shutdown.

Check authentication on the search endpoint, model and search-provider keys, outbound destination policy, query retention, rate limits, and administrative access. Confirm that the application does not expose a debug endpoint that reveals environment variables or provider credentials.

The 0 application count is a limitation of this measurement, not a conclusion about the population. The useful output is a verified list of search interfaces, their owner, and the data and provider authority behind each endpoint.

#9707. Prototype First: Test Your Idea in 30 Minutes Before You Spend Six Months Building It

Every developer knows the expensive question: is this idea worth six months of my life?

For most of us, the honest answer used to be "I don't know until I build it" — and building it was the six months. That equation is changing. AI coding agents can now turn a rough idea into a clickable, working prototype in well under an hour. The prototype won't be the product. But it can answer the question that matters most: should I build this at all?

That shift — from "build to find out" to "prototype to decide" — is quietly becoming the most valuable skill in AI-assisted development. Here's how to use it well.

A prototype has one job: to make the idea concrete enough to judge. It needs to answer three questions:

Notice what is not on that list: clean code, a design system, authentication, billing, tests, deployment pipelines. A prototype that has all of those is not a prototype — it's a product with a deadline you didn't need.

Here is the loop I use when an idea is worth testing but not yet worth committing to:

Before touching any agent, write a short brief in plain language:

Keep it under 150 words. If you can't describe the idea in a paragraph, the agent can't build it either — and that confusion is itself useful information.

Tell the agent explicitly that this is disposable: use the simplest stack, hardcode the data, skip auth, skip tests. A typical prompt looks like this:

The words "throwaway" and "stop when" matter. Without them, agents keep polishing — adding settings pages, refactoring, gold-plating — and your 30-minute test becomes a 3-hour project.

One of the biggest practical wins is running several agents at once, each on a different angle of the same idea: one builds the main flow, one tries a different UI approach, one attacks the risky integration. You compare the results and keep the best.

Three prototypes in 30 minutes tell you far more than one polished prototype in three hours, because the comparison itself is information: which approach felt natural, which one broke, which one a user understood without explanation.

A prototype sitting on your laptop has answered nothing. Show it to someone — a friend, a colleague, a user from the target audience — and watch them use it without guidance. The moments they pause, misclick, or ask "what does this do?" are the findings. Write them down verbatim; your memory will smooth them over by tomorrow.

The most common failure mode is the middle path: keeping the prototype and slowly turning it into the product. Prototype code is full of shortcuts that become permanent bugs. If the idea is worth building, it is worth rebuilding properly.

Being honest about the limits is what makes this workflow trustworthy rather than hype:

That last point is also the answer to the most common criticism of this style of working: that it produces developers who can't code. The skill hasn't disappeared; it has moved. It used to be writing every line. Now it's knowing what to ask for, recognising when the output is wrong, and understanding the system well enough to fix it. Developers who build on top of their own experience — their own libraries, their own hard-won knowledge of the domain — get far more out of agents than developers who start from zero, because they know what "good" looks like.

Prototype-first is not a tool choice. It's a habit: every idea gets a cheap test before it gets an expensive commitment. After a few months of it, you build a second skill on top — a sense for which ideas die in the prototype stage and which ones survive. That instinct is worth more than any single tool, because it protects the one resource you can't get back: the six months you would have spent on the wrong thing.

So the next time an idea excites you, resist the urge to start building it properly. Build it badly, quickly, in parallel — and let the prototype tell you whether it deserves the real thing.

The binary decide step is the strongest part, especially the warning against the middle path where a throwaway prototype slowly becomes production code. That drift usually starts when a demo goes well and the working version is kept 'just for now', so setting an explicit deletion date before the demo seems like a useful guardrail. How does the 30-minute loop handle ideas where the risky part is not the core interaction but integration with an existing system — is the happy path still the right first prototype, or should the integration spike come first? The one-paragraph brief looks like the cheapest filter here, because if the single action and the demo outcome are unclear, three parallel agents will simply produce three different interpretations of the same vague idea.

#9705. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

#9703. Building a Serverless Student Data App on AWS with S3, CloudFront, API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB

I recently built a small but complete serverless application on AWS: a web page where you can save a student's record and view everyone who has been saved. There are no servers to manage, no containers, and almost nothing billing when nobody is using it.

In this post I'll walk through how I put it together, the code I used, the mistakes I made along the way, and what I would change before calling it production-ready.

Who this is for: anyone with an AWS account who wants a hands-on first serverless project. You should be comfortable with the AWS console, basic Python (for Lambda) and basic JavaScript (for the frontend). Expect it to take roughly 45 minutes.

It's deliberately simple. The point isn't the app itself, it's seeing how a request travels through each AWS service from the browser to the database and back.

Behind that simple page is a chain of managed AWS services. The browser loads the page from CloudFront (backed by a private S3 bucket), then calls API Gateway directly:

The key idea is that the frontend and the API are separate. S3 and CloudFront only deliver the static page. Once it loads in the browser, the JavaScript calls API Gateway on its own, which is why CORS matters so much later in this post.

I built everything in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia) region. Keep all services in the same region to avoid confusing "why can't I see my table" moments. (CloudFront is global, but the S3 bucket, API, Lambda functions and table should all live in one region.)

I started with the data layer because everything else depends on it. The Lambda functions need a table to talk to, and the API needs functions to call, so building from the database outward keeps each step testable.

On-demand means I don't have to guess read/write capacity. I pay per request, which is ideal for a small project with unpredictable traffic.

A note on key design: studentid is the only key, so saving a student with an existing ID overwrites that record. That's fine here, but worth knowing. If you need to prevent accidental overwrites, you can add a condition to the write so it fails when the ID already exists.

Lambda needs permission to touch DynamoDB. Instead of putting credentials in code (never do that), I created an execution role. Lambda assumes this role when it runs, so the permissions travel with the function and nothing secret ends up in your source code.

To get moving quickly I attached the AWS managed AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess policy. It works, but it grants far more than this app needs. The proper least-privilege version is near the end of the post.

Also make sure the role can write logs to CloudWatch. The AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole managed policy does this, and you will want those logs when debugging. Without it, a failing function just fails silently and you have nothing to look at.

I created two Python functions, both using the role from Step 2. I used Lambda proxy integration in API Gateway, so each function receives the full HTTP request in event and must return a response with a status code, headers and a string body.

That last part is easy to get wrong: with proxy integration, API Gateway doesn't build the response for you. Whatever your function returns is exactly what the browser gets, including the CORS headers.

The code below shows the approach I used; adjust names to match your own setup.

This function reads the JSON body, checks the required fields, validates the age, and writes the item to DynamoDB. Bad input returns a 400, and anything unexpected returns a 500 without leaking internal details to the caller.

DynamoDB returns numbers as Python Decimal, which json.dumps can't serialize. This tripped me up, so the GET function needs a small converter. It also pages through the scan results, because a single scan call returns at most 1 MB of data.

Scan reads the whole table, which is fine for a small project but gets slow and expensive as data grows. I come back to this in the improvements list at the end.

Test before you connect anything. Before wiring up the API, test each function with a test event in the Lambda console. If it fails here, API Gateway will only make it harder to see why. For the POST function, a test event with an event.body containing a JSON string works well.

API Gateway is the public front door. It gives the browser an HTTPS URL and forwards each request to the right Lambda function.

After this step you should see three methods on the root resource: GET and POST (Lambda) and OPTIONS (Mock).

After deploying, you get an invoke URL that looks like this:

You can sanity-check it straight from a terminal before touching the frontend. The first command saves a student, the second lists everyone:

If both commands work, the backend is done. Everything from here on is about the browser.

This is where I lost the most time. The API worked perfectly in the console test and in curl, but the browser refused to show the result.

The reason is that the page and the API live on different origins (a CloudFront domain and an execute-api domain). Browsers send a preflight OPTIONS request before a cross-origin POST with a JSON body, and three things need to line up:

Miss any one of them and you'll see a CORS error in the browser console even though the API is healthy. That's what makes it so confusing: curl doesn't enforce CORS, so it keeps working while the browser fails.

Also remember that changes to API Gateway only take effect after you redeploy the stage.

The page is plain HTML and JavaScript. No framework needed. It has one form, two buttons, and a table that gets filled in from the API response.

The code below is the core logic. The screenshots in this post come from a version with extra CSS styling, so yours will look plainer until you add your own styles.

Replace the API_URL value with your own invoke URL from Step 4.

Using textContent instead of innerHTML for the table cells is a small habit that matters: it stops a student "name" like from running in someone's browser.

Here is the form after saving a student. The "Student Data Saved!" message comes straight from the Lambda response:

And here is the table after clicking View all Students:

Notice that student 2 appears before student 1. That isn't a bug in the page, it's how DynamoDB's Scan behaves, and I come back to it in the problems section.

#9702. GitHub Actions invalid workflow file on this ref

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at latchkey.dev

GitHub Actions invalid workflow file on this ref is the case where the same file passes on one branch and is rejected on another. A workflow is validated against the ref it runs on, and everything it pulls in resolves at that ref too, so a file you have not touched can become invalid.

The file is not validated once. Each ref is validated on its own, against whatever its references resolve to at that moment, and only the failing ref loses its check.

A required check never reports. The pull request sits with a check that is expected and never arrives, the merge button stays disabled, and nothing is red, because a run that dies during startup has no failing job to be red. Worse, the same workflow is demonstrably fine: it runs on the default branch and it ran on this branch last week. The only visible trace is a run in the Actions tab with a conclusion that is neither success nor failure, no jobs at all, and a single annotation naming your workflow file and a line number. That annotation is the entire diagnosis, and the pull request page does not show it.

```Invalid workflow file annotation, quoted from mosip/esignet#2551 Invalid workflow file: .github/workflows/push-trigger.yml#L88 The workflow is not valid. .github/workflows/push-trigger.yml (Line: 88, Col: 21): Invalid input, NODE_VERSION is not defined in the referenced workflow. .github/workflows/push-trigger.yml (Line: 89, Col: 16): Invalid input, ZIP_DIR is not defined in the referenced workflow.

When one branch validates and another does not, the difference is in the file or in what the file resolves to. A diff answers the first in one command; if the files are identical, a reference is floating.

```Terminal (illustrative) $ git diff origin/main..origin/release-2.0.x -- .github/workflows/

This file is written for this page and has never been run. Read on its own it is unremarkable: it calls a shared workflow at a moving ref and passes two inputs. It is valid the day it is written and stays valid until somebody in the other repository removes one of those inputs, at which point every ref still carrying this version becomes invalid and the updated refs do not.

```.github/workflows/ci.yml (illustrative) name: ci on: push: pull_request:

jobs: build: uses: octo-org/shared/.github/workflows/npm-build.yml@develop with: service: web node_version: "22" zip_dir: dist secrets: inherit

A run that fails during startup never creates a check run for any job, so branch protection has nothing to see. A check run that is expected is "waiting for a status to be reported", and the check suite carries startup_failure: "The check suite failed during startup. This status is not applicable to check runs."

The troubleshooting guide describes the same dead end from the merge box: when a required job never produces a check, "the pull request is blocked with \"Waiting for status to be reported.\"" It also lists the events whose checks are eligible at all, the other reason a check you can see in the Actions tab does not count: push, pull_request, pull_request_review, pull_request_target, deployment and deployment_status.

From the command line the state is easier to see. The GitHub CLI prints a run with no jobs and a failing conclusion as "This run likely failed because of a workflow file issue.", the nudge toward the annotation that the pull request page never gives you.

When the reference itself cannot be resolved rather than its inputs being wrong, the message is different: GitHub Actions reusable workflow was not found.

There is a run and it has nothing in it. Validation failed before any job was created, so there is no log to capture and no runner was ever involved. The annotation at the top is quoted from mosip/esignet#2551, which names the branch, the two lines and the run it came from.

Because each ref is validated on its own: the file on that branch, and everything it references resolved at that ref, has to be valid together. A caller pinned to a moving upstream ref can become invalid without anybody editing it, which is what mosip/esignet#2551 reported.

That the check suite failed before any job was created. The status reference defines it as "The check suite failed during startup. This status is not applicable to check runs." There are no jobs and no logs, only a run-level annotation naming the file and the line.

Because no check run was ever created for it. A check run in the expected state is "waiting for a status to be reported", and a workflow that dies at startup produces none, so branch protection waits forever.

Open the run itself rather than the pull request and read the annotation, or use the CLI, which prints "This run likely failed because of a workflow file issue." and the run URL. The annotation carries the file, the line and the column.

#9699. 🧠 Ego development 5: Fantasy Archetypes

Fantasy heroes are terrible org charts and excellent reading aids. Each Cook-Greuter stage gets an archetype, not to crown anyone, but to make the center of gravity visible: where you usually stand, who you borrow from under stress, and who you reach for when the room finally supports growth.

On the illustrations: Every figure is the same person at a different stage of life. The homogeneous look is deliberate; we are tracing one developmental arc, not assembling an ensemble cast.

The foundations piece named the mechanisms in prose. The visual atlas charted population, workplace tables, and contextual profiles. Then the series went fully pro: the developer at each stage, then Ego development 4: Your Delivery Manager's Stage. This piece comes fifth on purpose: after the applied profiles: a mnemonic companion so the stages stay sticky once the tables and role profiles are behind you.

Eight illustrations for E3→E10. In each one, the archetype you usually inhabit stands in front; earlier stages linger to the left, the next one to the right: where you might stretch on a good day or slip under stress. E2 appears only here in the series: the Brawler beside the Rogue, as regression floor, never as its own section.

The cast runs Brawler (E2 floor, beside E3) → Rogue → Soldier → Duelist → Crusader → Pathfinder → Grandmaster → Sage → Archangel. Fantasy names tempt crown-or-condemn readings; these are metaphors for memory, tied to center of gravity (where meaning-making usually lives, with room to wobble), in an arc of increasing light (narrative convenience, not moral ranking). E5's Duelist is modal; E10's Archangel is rare: neither lesser nor superior. Sample "types" in the literature (bull-headed blamer, loyalty-at-all-costs helper, visionary who can sacrifice for principle) map loosely onto Rogue / Soldier / Grandmaster; we keep fantasy faces, not sitcom cameos.

What follows: how to read the archetypes, then one section per stage: hook, Cook-Greuter reading, illustration. The prose stays on how the person constructs meaning; the developer and project-manager pieces already did the applied zoom.

The foundations and atlas already argue that stage is not a uniform label. Each illustration makes that visible: who you usually are in front, who you can still reach for, who you fall back to.

Cook-Greuter's SCTi reports a total protocol rating: your habitual center of gravity, not a coordinate frozen under all conditions. On Cook-Greuter's N=4,510 sample (dissertation, Table 3), those centers cluster at E4–E6; the atlas charts the distribution. What the instrument captures is where meaning-making usually lives, the way a planet's orbit has a barycenter even when the path wobbles.

In practice, the wobble is large. Under stress, identity threat, fatigue, or conflict, most adults drop one to two stages without deciding to: documented regression, not hypocrisy. In a holding environment with enough support and developmental density, the same person can operate above center for stretches. Stage is contagious in both directions; the tavern gets louder when the Brawler enters, and quieter when the Sage does, even if neither is anyone's permanent address.

The foundations piece keeps organizational regression in prose (agile E6 mutating into command-and-control E4 under crisis). Here we focus on the individual range the atlas previously diagrammed abstractly: now readable as faces beside each habitual stage.

Each stage adds capacities; it does not uninstall the old ones. An E6 Crusader can still perform Soldier conformity or Duelist competitiveness when useful: registers to deploy, not cages to escape. Regression is the exception: you drop a level without choosing it, the way a tavern fight chooses you back.

The figures brighten from E3 onward, Rogue to Archangel, because the arc matches Cook-Greuter's construction-then-deconstruction curve, not because later heroes are "better people." The foundations piece is explicit: not a ladder of moral worth. Knowing the model won't raise your stage; slapping a Crusader sticker on your laptop definitely will not.

Give someone a luminous archetype and the ego will wear it as armor, especially E5, where expertise already doubles as identity. These names explain patterns ("that's Duelist optimization, not systemic leverage") and anchor memory after the harder work of observing behavior. If the image replaces the reading, you have rebuilt the very badge the series argues against: just with better art.

E2 (on the left) is the exception that proves the professional layout: pre-moral impulse, not part of the light arc; and the only place in this series it gets a face. Adult samples in Cook-Greuter's data don't center on E2, so it never gets its own professional section. It appears here only as the Brawler: developmental floor and regression target when stress strips opportunistic control back to raw reaction. (Regression is the one move you don't get to cosplay.)

E2 as floor archetype: the Brawler: tavern scuffle, raised fists, bodies colliding now, no tomorrow in the swing. Cook-Greuter's Impulsive (E2): impulse rules the moment; discipline is only what others impose ("be mean to me and I'll hit back"). No stable causal exploitation yet: things happen; strategy arrives at E3. Good and evil, if they appear at all, collapse into immediate want: are you giving me what I need right now? This is pre-moral, not the gray morality of the Rogue: no con artistry, just the fist before the scheme. Not a glamorous anti-hero: raw reaction, a bar brawl in the moment.

E3 archetype: the Rogue (in the middle): con artist, renegade, grifter. In fantasy/D&D usage, rogue spans spy, scout, pirate: operating outside norms, not looting chests for sport. Charm is a tool; loyalty is temporary; the smile lasts exactly as long as the angle does.

Cook-Greuter reading: E3 is Self-Centric: impulses are partly controlled, but control serves don't get caught. Causality is understood well enough to exploit: route blame, bend rules off-camera, treat people as tools. Morality is cost/benefit; trust is instrumental. A sharp Rogue can give the loyal speech and cut the rope in the same scene. High-risk is the daring face of the same seat: the courage can be real, and the center is still the personal win. Observable marker at work: "It's not me, it's them." This is the gray moral floor of our light arc, not a villain, an opportunist. The Rogue is where the redemption story starts, not because they are evil, but because consequence has become a game board.

But E4, the soldier (on the right), is around the corner.

Archetype: the Soldier, standing where the line says stand. A foot soldier with a face, but the same face as everyone in the line, belonging before rank, oath, or command. Belonging is the self: approval soothes, exclusion wounds, and the group's "we" answers questions the person has not yet learned to ask alone.

Cook-Greuter reading: E4 is Group-Centric: group rules are reality, not choices to examine. Belonging is identity; shame (others' gaze) outweighs guilt (inner voice). Deviation threatens the self. At work: "That's how it's done here." Strength: reliable execution inside stable boundaries. Limit: the frame cannot question itself: innovation that disturbs the group feels like disloyalty, the organizational equivalent of lighting a candle in the scriptorium and being asked to leave.

These people have identity; the uniform wears one silhouette. The figure in front is your habitual stage; the others are the range you still carry.

Archetype: the Duelist: skilled, visible, numerous: the modal fighter you actually meet in the square. Competence is identity: win the exchange, look sharp doing it, and treat every challenge as a chance to prove the craft still holds.

Cook-Greuter reading: E5 is Skill-Centric: the modal adult stage where most of the population stops (~37% center of gravity in Cook-Greuter's Table 3 sample). Introspection appears but stays defended behind expertise: "No one can tell me anything I don't already know." The older name Expert names that identity. The duel can be real craft, or only the costume of craft. Motivation shifts to recognition: titles, KPIs, being seen as competent. They optimize the square, not the board. Observable marker: "It depends on the context, doesn't it?": a genuine opening, not yet systemic sight.

Most professionals you meet are Duelists still learning whether the duel was worth scheduling.

Archetype: the Crusader: cause chosen, not inherited with the title. Order joined by conviction; responsibility worn as purpose. Missionary certainty is the shadow: the same integrity that delivers can also filibuster anything that threatens the code.

Cook-Greuter reading: E6 is Self-Determining: rules become self-chosen standards. Guilt is internal; long-term goals appear; remote-proof self-discipline lands here. At work: "That's on me, I'll fix it." They seek feedback, challenge authority on principle, and can become the most effective blocker of transformation precisely because their arguments are principled and technically impeccable: the Crusader who will filibuster the retrofit because the retrofit violates the code they adopted.

Archetype: the Pathfinder: off the wall, mapping where the group's cartography ends. Leaves the rank voluntarily; solo clarity is the gift and the trap: they see the blind spots early, then struggle to bring anyone else along the new trail.

Cook-Greuter reading: E7 is Self-Questioning: the frame shows up as a frame, roles relativized, systemic dysfunction named early. Two expressions of one structure. The Individualist turns inward. The Pluralist takes the map apart in public and treats every voice as equally valid. Contradictions appear and do not rank themselves yet; stable paradox arrives at E8. Cook-Greuter calls this stage disillusionment: old rewards (KPIs, promotions, belonging) stop working before new integration stands. The valley is real: insight without leverage, authenticity without a team. Solo delivery of a hard objective is plausible; moving others is not yet. Observable marker: "There are several ways to see this."

A guide at the edge of the map: restless, lucid, still carrying the loneliness of the valley.

Archetype: the Grandmaster: behind the line, not on it. Someone who has lived the fight and no longer needs to win it personally. Presence without performance: the room moves because conditions shifted, not because a speech landed.

Cook-Greuter reading: E8 is Self-Actualizing, opposing tensions integrated; trust and control, autonomy and accountability, held as design choices. Paradox is now part of the territory, and not every voice ranks the same. The Grandmaster creates conditions: one maneuver that retires ten battles. Elected leadership of the collective, not dynastic throne. Misread from below as idle or indecisive because impact is silent: the lever moved off-screen while everyone else counts sword swings. The stage's own shadow is different from that misread. The Crusader wanted the cleanest victory. The Grandmaster wants the company to become what it can, and will hurry anyone who walks too slowly toward that. A holy quest pursued as a score still belongs here. Humility that proves the wisdom, and a hard time putting down "higher is better," stay in the same shadow.

Ego-less leadership in one frame: Soldiers still hold the visible line; the Grandmaster is not another face in the rank. Orchestration without the throne: the fight is no longer about proving armor.

Archetype: the Sage: sees the game as a game, including the game of being the sage. Quiet from across the room; the gift is naming the construct, not a costume of calm.

Cook-Greuter reading: E9 is Construct-Aware, a differentiation, not a peace treaty. Fifth-person perspective: meaning, goals, and the ego show up as constructs. Two foci. Construct-aware builds a still larger map. Ego-aware, the name she prefers for the stage in the full-spectrum paper, notices the map-maker cannot step outside the want for a map. Language can be complex and raw. From across the room that looks simple, which is why the Sage is mistaken for a checked-out Duelist. Catalyzes, then withdraws: success is making yourself dispensable, without needing the credit to prove who you are. Discriminating test: can they name the construct, including their own, when the moment demands it? A calm that needs no proof is the Archangel, or a costume.

Archetype: the Archangel: Saint Michael register: seasoned, someone who has fought long enough to stop needing the fight. Luminous, free, intermittently present. Acts, then disappears: intervenes without angling for credit.

Cook-Greuter reading: E10 is Unitive, the witnessing seat, and a catch-all: sentence completions never split the ego-transcendent territory cleanly, so later extensions (O'Fallon, Commons) sit beyond this horizon rather than inside a finished stage. Evaluation and control loosen; seriousness and triviality alternate without forcing resolution; people are accepted as they are, and later stages are not ranked as better. Speech can be very simple, the opposite of the Sage's elaborate seeing-through. A peak hour of non-attachment is a state, not this center of gravity. Non-attachment enables direct action rather than blocking it. Observable flavor: "Does any of this ultimately matter? Also, shall we ship it?" Rare in professional samples: treat as horizon, not hiring target. Ironist is Torbert's label; Cook-Greuter dropped it because readers misread it.

Total freedom, does what is needed without gripping the outcome, and capacity to vanish align with lets go of evaluating and controlling and makes yourself dispensable. The Archangel completes the arc of light; the Brawler floor is far behind and only visits under regression. At E10, there is nothing ahead: only the trail behind.

Brawler → Rogue → Soldier → Duelist → Crusader → Pathfinder → Grandmaster → Sage → Archangel: Cook-Greuter's construction-then-deconstruction arc, read as increasing light, not increasing worth. The figure in front is habitual gravity; the faces beside it, repertoire and regression. The foundations and atlas carry the mechanics; this piece carries the mnemonic.

It searches for malware and compares code, theme, and plugin files with the records in the WordPress.org repository to verify their integrity and reports changes to you.

Wordfence security scanner provides you with actionable insights into your website's security status and will alert you to any potential threats, keeping it safe and secure. It also includes login security features that let you activate reCAPTCHA and two-factor authentication for your website.

Akismet can help prevent spam from appearing on your site. Every day, it automatically checks every comment against a global database of spam to block malicious content. With Akismet, you also won’t have to worry about innocent comments being caught by the filter or false positives. You can simply tell Akismet about those and it will get better over time. It also checks your contact form submissions against its global spam database and weed out unnecessary fake information.

Contact Form 7 is a plug-in that allows you to create contact forms that make it easy for your users to send messages to your site. The plug-in was developed by Takayuki Miyoshi and lets you create multiple contact forms on the same site; it also integrates Akismet spam filtering and lets you customize the styling and fields that you want to use in the form. The plug-in provides CAPTCHA and Ajax submitting.

When you’re looking for an easy way to manage your Google Analytics-related web tracking services, Monster Insights can help. It’s same as Google Analytics

It is a powerful tool to keep track of your traffic stats. With it, you can view stats for your active sessions, conversions, and bounce rates. You’ll also be able to see your total revenue, the products you sell, and how your site is performing when it comes to referrals.

MonsterInsights offers a free plan that includes basic Google Analytics integration, data insights, and user activity metrics.

Pretty links also helps you to automatically shorten your url for your post and pages.

But when we do get the chance, we want a slam-dunk recipe — or 12. Here’s a dozen of the favorite fall recipes we’ll be making this month: from pumpkin cake bars to spooky fudge brownies to a crowd-pleasing vegetarian quiche.

It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown! Only this version comes in cake form. The decoration is deceptively easy: Stack two small Bundts, frost the entire thing, and add a chocolate-dipped ice cream cone for the stem.

A bit of bread flour and vital wheat gluten give these whole wheat rolls a lofty rise, while the milk, butter, and honey create a plush crumb that stays soft for days. Add a salted honey butter wash to the tops of a freshly baked batch, and you may not have any leftover.

Get the recipe: Super-Soft Whole Wheat Rolls

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Golden Wheat Flour and Bread Flour

"Tassie" means "small cup" in Scottish, and these dainty pecan pies pack a nutty punch. The cream cheese pastry crust is cut into rounds and placed in a mini muffin pan before the pecan pie filling is spooned into each well. With only 30 minutes of hands-on time, these two dozen tassies come together quickly on a crisp fall afternoon.

#9695. Apache HTTP/2 vulnerability CVE-2026-119618: find every h2 line, upgrade to 2.4.71, check the running process

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at systemdesignsimple.com

The Apache HTTP/2 vulnerability CVE-2026-119618 is a critical mod_http2 flaw in Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 that, according to the Apache advisory of 2026-11-11, can lead to remote code execution on a build that offers HTTP/2 (h2 or h2c). Upgrade to 2.4.71 or your distro's fixed httpd and mod_http2 packages, do a full restart, and confirm the process serving traffic loaded the new build. If you cannot upgrade today, remove h2 and h2c from every effective Protocols line.

This guide is for Apache servers you own or maintain.

You are affected when three things hold for the running server: the httpd or mod_http2 build is in the range without a distro backport, http2_module is loaded, and an effective Protocols line offers h2 (HTTP/2 over TLS) or h2c (HTTP/2 over cleartext TCP). That line can sit in the main config, one , or a file pulled in by Include or IncludeOptional.

Run the dumps the way the service runs httpd: same executable, same -f, -d and -D arguments, same environment. Read those from the unit first. On Debian, apachectl loads /etc/apache2/envvars for you; a bare apache2 -M does not.

The grep finds candidates. A hit inside or only counts when that condition is true for this service, so read each hit in its scope.

On packaged builds the module may not come from the httpd package. On RHEL, Rocky, Alma and Fedora, mod_http2 ships as its own mod_http2 package, so find the owner of the loaded .so and compare that revision with the distro advisory:

For the official container image, pulling changes nothing that is already running. Pull, recreate the container the way your deployment does it, then check inside the replacement:

On a host, test the config and do a full stop and start. A graceful restart replaces the children but keeps the parent, which can keep the old binary mapped.

A (deleted) mapping means the process still runs files the package manager replaced. An empty result only means nothing stale is mapped. Whether the build is fixed comes from the package revision check above.

An HTTP/2 stream is one request and response carried on a shared connection. mod_http2 reads each stream on the main connection and collects its headers into an h2_request allocated from the stream's pool (h2_stream.c in 2.4.70). An APR pool is the arena allocator that owns an httpd object's memory. The stream is then processed on a secondary connection, where c2_process() builds an ordinary request_rec.

assign_headers() does that hand-off. It first clones the stream's header table into r->headers_in, which the request owns. One later branch, for a request with a Content-Type, no Content-Length and no body, sets Content-Length: 0. In 2.4.70 that write went to req->headers, the table still owned by the stream. The fix commit points it at r->headers_in.

So request-side code changes stream-side state. APR tables have no locking, and adding an entry can allocate from the owning pool. The advisory classifies this as concurrent use of a shared resource without proper synchronization and says it can lead to RCE, which here means a remote client's code running as the httpd worker user. It does not describe the corruption sequence, and we do not claim one.

Our lab, apache-http2-check-lab, classifies configurations; it never starts httpd or sends a request. It builds 15 throwaway hosts, each with a sample httpd -v, apachectl -V and httpd.conf, and follows Include into directories and wildcards. In our test on 2026-11-13 (Node 22.13.1, 305 ms), it classified all 8 synthetic in-range fixtures with h2 or h2c as affected, including h2 only inside vhost *:8443 and h2c reached through Include conf/extra, a directory. No vulnerability reproduction was performed.

Each "after" applies one change: the upgrade, or removing h2 and h2c from every Protocols line. A half fix that dropped h2 but kept h2c stayed affected, since h2c still reaches mod_http2.

The lab never runs httpd, so it shows neither the race nor that 2.4.71 removes it; that rests on the advisory and the commit. Its parser lowercases module and protocol names, so the HTTP2_module fixture describes a config a real httpd would refuse to load: count 7 real configurations plus one parser case. The 2026-11-13 run also let the last Protocols line in a scope replace earlier ones, which httpd does not do; the lab code now adds them up. It reads files on disk, not the running process or distro changelogs.

The advisory names no workaround. Turning HTTP/2 off reduces exposure, because no connection reaches mod_http2:

Repeated Protocols directives in one scope accumulate protocols. Adding Protocols http/1.1 after Protocols h2 leaves h2 enabled; edit or remove every earlier h2/h2c entry (set_protocols() in core.c).

Or unload the module (sudo a2dismod http2 on Debian, or comment out LoadModule http2_module), then apachectl -t, a full restart, and apachectl -M showing no http2_module. Then test each origin listener directly, not through a CDN or proxy. --resolve keeps Host and SNI (the hostname a TLS client sends) correct; --noproxy '*' skips proxy variables.

The direct test sends HTTP/2 with no HTTP/1.1 step, so a server without h2c answers it with an error rather than 1.1 (curl docs). H2Upgrade and H2Direct control the two cleartext paths separately, so run both. A connection refused or certificate error is inconclusive. If the before-run already prints 1.1, check curl -V | grep HTTP2.

For holding a fixed release you cannot deploy yet, the OWASP Vulnerable Dependency Management cheat sheet covers the cases. Directive details are in the Protocols docs.

assign_headers() clones the stream's headers so the request owns private state, then one write goes to the original. The const on req did not catch it, because the table pointer inside the struct is not const. If you maintain C modules that hand data between threads, search for writes through the source struct after a clone.

On RHEL-family hosts, httpd -v and rpm -q httpd describe one package while the vulnerable code can live in another. A ticket that checks only the server version can close with the module unchanged. We would close it only when the package owning the loaded mod_http2.so matches the distro advisory and the restarted PID shows no stale mappings.

Our own lab got httpd's parsing wrong in two places. Any config scanner carries that risk, since its verdicts depend on how closely it copies the server's parser. We now start from DUMP_INCLUDES, the include tree httpd resolves itself, and end with a direct curl to each origin listener. The OpenSSH bypass check used the same /proc step, the Apache OFBiz check found a version file that could not tell patched from unpatched, and the Node.js Brotli check follows the same order.

#9694. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9691. How I Built and Shut Down an AI-Coded Sports Trivia Game

Sam Brovda (Samuel Brovda) comes from the sales world and builds software on the side with AI coding agents.

Sam Brovda (Samuel Brovda) comes from the sales world and builds software on the side with AI coding agents.

Sam Brovda (Samuel Brovda) comes from the sales world and builds software on the side with AI coding agents.

I’m not an engineer. I come from the sales world. But between June 18 and July 16, I pushed 172 commits to a side project called statback.

Most of those commits list an AI coding agent as co-author. 155 of them carry a “Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8” line. So this isn’t a story about me learning to code. It’s about what happens when you ship fast with an agent, and the bugs that show up when you do.

Statback is a daily sports trivia game. Every day you get a binder page of nine card backs: a 3x3 grid. The name is redacted. So are the birthplace and, at first, the team. You get the stat lines. Your job is to name the player.

Everyone gets the same board. Wordle and Immaculate Grid were the model. The product doc says so. There’s no timer. You get three tries per card. Hints are there if you need them, but they cost you points.

It started with baseball. By the end of day one it had MLB, NBA, and NFL. Every card you name goes into your binder. There are rookie cards, foil parallels, serial numbers, and print runs. A Gold parallel really is limited to 10 per drop.

The stack: Next.js, Supabase, Vercel, PostHog, Resend for email, and web push.

The first day’s commits read like a roadmap. Build the game. Vintage clubhouse UI. A binder that swings open. Pull lineups from the MLB Stats API. Monthly leaderboard. Magic-link accounts. Google sign-in. NBA. NFL. Holo card finishes. Real jersey numbers.

That’s one day of commit history. With an agent that’s possible. It’s also how you end up with a long list of fixes.

Hints were the hardest part. I rebuilt them over and over.

On June 19, a commit said “Make every hint factually valid (no unverified accolades).” On June 20, I swapped out hints that just repeated the stats for new trivia generated by Claude. That covered 888 of the 930 players in the pool. Later that day one hint had a stray {“placeholder”:false} stuck to the front of it. It was an AI output artifact that got into the live text.

On June 21 I threw the hints out again and rebuilt them from Wikipedia and Wikidata. 914 of the 930 players got grounded clues.

On July 16, the last commit in the repo was still about hints. Once the team column showed on every card, the scouting-report hints were naming the player’s own team on 60% of entries. The hint said exactly what the card already showed.

Takeaway: an AI will produce content fast. It won’t check that content against what’s already on screen. You have to do that.

I changed the daily difficulty mix at least five times.

First a 3/4/2 split (easy/medium/hard) with a guaranteed “white whale.” Then 2/4/3. Then a recalibration that re-rolled the board people were already playing that day. I reverted it. Then I added a fix that pins each daily lineup the first time it’s served, so live and past boards can’t change. Then I re-applied the recalibration. Then a 1/3/3/2 spread.

On July 3, the analytics said I’d gone too far. Per the commit, PostHog showed average hints per board jumped from about 4 to about 12. Perfect 9/9 boards dropped from about 41% to about 20%. So I dialed it back to a mostly modern 2/2/4/1 spread.

Takeaway: ship the analytics before you tune. That’s the only reason I knew I’d overshot.

Here’s a commit message from June 24: “CRITICAL: stop the store-wipe bug.”

The problem: a failed database read was treated as an empty store. Then a fallback write could overwrite the whole database with empty defaults. The commit calls that the root cause of a data wipe.

Within the next 40 minutes, three more commits went in. A guard that blocks any write that would cut the core data in half. Hourly snapshots of the store in a 48-slot ring. And a plan to move off one big JSON document onto real tables.

Two days later, a performance commit named the same root cause for slow gameplay. Everything lived in a single ~1MB JSON doc. Every write competed for one row.

Takeaway: the agent will happily build you a shortcut architecture. It works until real people use it. Ask early how your data is stored and what happens when a read fails.

On June 27: “Fix phone overheating from foil shimmer.” The shiny animation on rare cards was looping a CSS variable that forced constant full repaints. It looked great and it cooked phones.

Same day, I fixed cards flipping backwards when you opened them. Twice. The first fix wasn’t enough.

Sharing is how a daily game spreads, so I kept changing it. On June 20 alone: share a link that unfurls an image of the stat line. Share each card as its own link. Then switch to plain text plus a link, because, per the commit, recipients preferred readable text over an image.

The next day I learned that X and iMessage cache link previews for days. So share URLs got a version number to force a refresh.

Later, every share link started carrying a referral code. Both people get a “Scout” foil card when a friend joins.

The pace is real. Three sports, accounts, leaderboards, collecting, email reminders, an admin panel, and referrals, all in about a month.

But speed creates its own cleanup. A lot of my commit history is fixing what I built. Hints, difficulty, data safety, performance, sharing. None of those fixes are fancy. They come from watching the product and the numbers, then telling the agent exactly what’s wrong.

In the end I shut statback down. Maintaining it was a headache, and it was a side project. Every fix opened up another one.

But it taught me a lot. How to work with an agent. What breaks when real people show up. What to check before I trust what it built.

It’s the reason I’m where I am now, building a real project: a consumer mobile app. Statback was the practice run.

#9687. Bothy: Building Verifiable AI Decisions With Arweave Receipts

Every winter, somewhere in the UK, a person with a pager has to decide whether to close a mountain road. Picture a Cumbria County Council winter duty officer with the A5094 and the B5311 on their desk: narrow, steep, single-lane passes that ice fast and plough badly. Close too early and you strand a valley of commuters and farms. Close too late and a family of four meets a snowdrift on a blind bend.

The Met Office warnings, the gritting schedule, the gradient map and the incident history all exist, scattered across systems that were never joined. The officer has to hold it all in their head under a deadline and be personally accountable for the call.

That is the decision Bothy is built for. It is an open-source, evidence-first agent. It watches a curated evidence graph (Met Office warnings, live weather, route topology, incident records) and produces a cited risk assessment: a score, a label, a draft for the duty officer, and the reasoning chain behind every claim, each linked to a real data point. Then it does what dashboards don't: it hands the decision to a named human, who approves or rejects it, and it keeps the whole trail.

The same agent has a second surface. For supply-chain analysts it produces defence briefs, cited investigations of what would happen to a logistics programme if a dependency went dark, reviewed by a named reviewer before anything counts as decided.

The interesting problem here isn't the AI. It's what happens after.

Every "AI safety" feature in every dashboard I've seen asks you to take the vendor's word for it. The model says it cited. The platform says it audited. The log says the approval happened. But when a duty officer's name goes on a closure, or an analyst's name goes on a risk call, the question that matters is: can anyone independently verify that this exact output existed at this exact time, and that nobody edited it before the human signed?

Usually the evidence behind a decision evaporates. Logs rotate, dashboards version, decisions get re-edited. So my answer this week was to stop asking for trust and start publishing fingerprints.

At the two moments that matter, when the agent generates an output and when a human decides on it, Bothy anchors a SHA-256 receipt to Arweave mainnet. The record itself never leaves our systems. Only its fingerprint does, permanently.

Here is one minted by the production deployment:

Open the case link and click Verify. Your browser fetches the anchored receipt, recomputes the fingerprint of the record on screen with crypto.subtle, and compares the two. My server is not trusted for the answer, and that is the whole point.

A receipt on generation proves the AI's output existed, unaltered, at time T. That is table stakes.

The second moment is the human decision. The decision receipt chains back to the generation receipt (subjectDigest plus generationTx), records the decision and its timestamp, and stores the reviewer's identity only as a hash: committed, not revealed. On the defence-brief side it also pins the head of the case's hash-chained audit log.

So the anchored statement isn't "an AI said X on Tuesday." It is "a named responsibility-holder signed off on X on Wednesday, and the audit trail behind it hashes to this value." If anyone later edits the brief, the draft or the log, recomputation fails loudly.

This was the subtle part. The naive version, sha256(JSON.stringify(assessment)), doesn't survive contact with a real database. Postgres real columns round-trip a few ulps off the in-memory value, jsonb doesn't preserve key order, and fields like status and decidedAt legitimately change after anchoring.

So the digest covers a canonical payload: immutable fields only, keys sorted recursively, scores rounded to four decimals.

Because the agent and the browser share the same canonicalization module, a judge recomputing in devtools gets the same fingerprint the server anchored. It is tamper-evident by construction, not by promise.

Three things went wrong on the way here, and they're worth more to readers than the wins.

The duty officer's problem isn't "AI." It's that when their name goes on a closure, the proof of why usually disappears. Bothy makes that impossible by design: the agent produces the draft, the human owns the call, and Arweave holds the receipt. The accountability belongs to the person. The proof belongs to nobody. It's just there, permanently, for anyone to check.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

#9682. Custodial vs. Non-Custodial vs. Self-Hosted Crypto Payment Gateways

Writing about crypto payment infrastructure: custody, stablecoins, webhooks, and what it really takes to run payments in production.

Writing about crypto payment infrastructure: custody, stablecoins, webhooks, and what it really takes to run payments in production.

Writing about crypto payment infrastructure: custody, stablecoins, webhooks, and what it really takes to run payments in production.

Adding a crypto checkout to a website takes an afternoon now. What takes longer, and what most merchants never stop to think about, is where the money actually sits after a customer pays.

There are three basic answers: the gateway holds it, the gateway watches while you hold it, or you run the whole thing yourself. There are variations in between, of course. But each approach trades convenience for control in a different way, and the trade usually becomes visible only when something goes wrong.

I spent a while on the operations side of a payment gateway. Merchants asked about fees, supported coins, and how fast the plugin installs. Almost nobody asked who could freeze their balance. That question showed up later, in support tickets.

So here is the comparison I wish more people saw before they picked a provider.

This is a common model for plug-and-play crypto gateways. The customer pays to an address the provider controls. You see a balance in a dashboard, and you withdraw when the provider’s rules allow it.

The upside is real. You don’t touch private keys, you don’t watch the blockchain, and you don’t have to figure out how to move tokens between wallets. Someone else matches payments to orders and tells your store when an invoice is paid. For a small business, that’s a lot of work taken off the table.

The downside is that the balance on your screen is a claim on money held by someone else, not money in a wallet you control.

Withdrawals can come with minimums, fees, limits, and sometimes a manual review when an amount looks unusual. If the provider restricts your account, has an outage, or shuts down, you may have no immediate way to access those funds.

Anyone who has run a business on card payments knows this feeling. Payment processors can hold merchant balances during disputes or risk reviews. Crypto doesn’t automatically remove that dependency. It can simply move it to a different company.

Pricing usually follows the payment amount. Providers often take a percentage of each transaction, with withdrawal or network fees added depending on the service.

It’s convenient, especially at the beginning. But the convenience comes with a question worth answering: how much money are you comfortable leaving with a third party?

A different approach is the non-custodial gateway. Here, the provider handles payment detection and order updates, but the money goes directly to wallets controlled by the merchant.

Some services use an extended public key, or xpub, to generate receiving addresses. Others connect to merchant-controlled wallet addresses through different methods. With an xpub-based setup, the gateway can generate a fresh address for each order, monitor incoming transactions, and notify your store when the payment arrives. It doesn’t need your private key to do that.

The benefit is straightforward. The gateway cannot hold your balance or stop you from moving funds out of your own wallet. If its website disappears tomorrow, the crypto already received is still accessible through your wallet.

There’s an important distinction here, though. Controlling your keys doesn’t mean every asset is impossible to freeze. Stablecoin issuers such as Tether can restrict tokens at the address level. That’s an issuer-level risk, not gateway custody, but merchants should understand the difference.

And removing the gateway from custody doesn’t remove all the work. A few things become your responsibility:

None of these issues makes non-custodial payments a bad choice. But the work has to land somewhere. If the gateway isn’t moving the money for you, your team, your wallet software, or another service has to handle it. That’s easy to overlook when you’re comparing checkout screenshots.

Then there’s the self-hosted route. Tools like BTCPay Server let businesses operate their own payment infrastructure. You can run your own server and blockchain node, connect your own wallet, and process payments without paying a traditional gateway’s transaction commission.

For on-chain Bitcoin payments, private keys can stay outside the payment server, including in a hardware wallet. That’s an important advantage. Running the payment software doesn’t have to mean keeping the keys that control your funds on a public-facing server.

But self-hosting brings a different set of responsibilities. Someone has to keep the infrastructure running, install updates, maintain backups, check synchronization, and notice when something stops working.

And then there’s everything that doesn’t fit neatly into the payment software. What happens when a customer pays after an invoice expires? Who handles a partial payment? What if the customer needs a refund? What if they send the correct token on the wrong network? Software can help with these situations. It doesn’t make the business decisions for you.

The cost is also easy to misunderstand. No gateway commission doesn’t mean zero cost. You still have hosting expenses, blockchain network fees, and the time spent maintaining the system.

For a company with engineers who already manage infrastructure, self-hosting can be a great fit. For a shop with three people and no developer, it can feel like running a second business just to accept payments.

Yes, through custody and withdrawal controls

Payment tracking may stop, but funds stay accessible

Wallet management, consolidation, network fees

Infrastructure, security, payment operations

Transaction percentages, possible withdrawal fees

Transaction fees, subscriptions, or fixed pricing

The provider, for the addresses it tracks

No external gateway, but on-chain data is public

There’s no universally correct column. A business processing a handful of payments a month has different needs from a platform receiving thousands every day. The mistake is assuming these three models offer the same kind of control just because they all put a crypto payment button on a website.

Here’s something that tends to get overlooked regardless of which model you choose: crypto addresses outlive checkouts.

A customer receives an address for an invoice, saves it somewhere, and uses it again three months later. Maybe they copied it into an accounting system. Maybe their finance team saved it as a trusted destination. Whatever the reason, they don’t know you’ve stopped using it.

Marking an address as “retired” in your application changes nothing on the blockchain. The address can still receive funds, and those funds still need to be accounted for.

October 2026 gave us a painful example. Indian crypto exchange CoinDCX confirmed a loss of 15.99 million USDT connected to wallet infrastructure it had deprecated after a security incident in July 2025.

According to CoinDCX, some customers kept depositing funds into old addresses. An automated service was supposed to move those deposits into secure wallets, but it stopped working for a period. Funds accumulated, and the company eventually reported the loss. CoinDCX said it absorbed the amount and that customer balances were unaffected.

There is another side to the story. On-chain investigator ZachXBT reported that one of the old deposit addresses was still being used and swept as recently as April and May 2026, raising questions about how completely the old infrastructure had actually been retired. Not every part of the explanation is settled.

But the broader lesson is hard to miss. An address doesn’t stop working because your internal system says it should.

An exchange isn’t an online store, and the scale here is obviously different. Still, the problem can appear in any business that creates payment addresses and later stops watching them. If customers can keep sending funds to an address, who detects those payments? Who still controls the keys? Who moves the money? And how do you know the system responsible for doing that is actually running?

It’s not enough to retire an address in a database. You need a plan for what happens afterward.

Before connecting a gateway to your store, I’d ask these questions:

You probably won’t find all these answers on a pricing page. Some require reading documentation. Others require asking support a few uncomfortable questions. I’d rather ask them before the first payment than after a withdrawal gets stuck.

Crypto checkout has become easy enough that custody can feel like a minor implementation detail. It isn’t.

A gateway that holds your funds offers convenience but creates a dependency. Keeping the keys yourself removes that layer of custody, while leaving you responsible for more of the operational work. Running your own infrastructure gives you the most control, but also means taking responsibility when something breaks. And regardless of the model, old addresses, network fees, payment records, and failure recovery still need someone paying attention.

The point isn’t that every merchant should become their own payment processor. It’s that every merchant should know who controls the money after the customer hits Pay.

Writing about crypto payment infrastructure: custody, stablecoins, webhooks, and what it really takes to run payments in production.
